body.en: Good statistical conclusions require well-designed data collection. Observational studies describe associations; experiments can establish cause and effect. Randomisation is the key tool for eliminating bias.

MethodProcedureKey point
Simple Random (SRS)Every group of \(n\) equally likelyUnbiased, gold standard
Stratified RandomSRS within each stratumReduces variability; must cover all strata
ClusterRandomly select whole clustersCheaper; cluster must mirror population
SystematicEvery \(k\)-th from random startEasy; avoid periodic patterns
ConvenienceWhoever is handyUsually biased — avoid
Voluntary responsePeople choose to respondStrong-opinion bias — avoid

Randomise — assign subjects to treatments randomly to eliminate confounding.

Replicate — use enough subjects so real effects can be detected.

Control — use a control group (placebo or standard treatment); hold all other variables constant.

Block — group similar subjects into blocks before randomising; reduces unexplained variability (like stratified sampling for experiments).

Placebo effect — improvement due to belief in treatment. Use blinding (subjects unaware of treatment) or double-blinding (neither subjects nor researchers know).

Confounding variable — associated with both the explanatory and response variables; may produce a spurious association. Randomisation controls for known and unknown confounders.

Observational study vs. experiment — only experiments with random assignment can establish causation.

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Sampling & Experimentation

body.en:
• Correlation vs. Causation: Observational studies can ONLY establish association or correlation between variables. You CANNOT infer cause-and-effect without random assignment of treatments in a controlled experiment.
  • Defining a Confounding Variable: On FRQs, to successfully identify a confounder, you must explain: (1) how the variable is associated with the explanatory group, AND (2) how it affects the response variable.
  • Stratified Sampling vs. Blocking: Students often confuse these terms. Stratification is a sampling method (choosing subjects from a population). Blocking is an experimental design strategy (grouping similar subjects before random assignment to reduce within-treatment variability).
  • Scope of Inference: Random selection from the population allows generalizing results to that population. Random assignment to treatment groups allows drawing causal conclusions. If you have neither, conclusions apply only to the study participants and cannot claim causation!

problem.en: A clinical trial randomly assigns 200 patients to Drug A or placebo. Neither patients nor doctors know who gets which. Classify the design and identify its features.

solution.en:
This is a completely randomised, double-blind experiment.

Blinding: patients don't know → controls placebo effect. Double-blind: doctors don't know → prevents researcher bias in assessment.

Since subjects were randomly assigned, a statistically significant difference in outcomes can be attributed to the drug (causation). However, without a random sample from the population, generalisation to all patients is limited.

problem.en: A stratified random sample selects 10 students from each year level (9–12) at a school. Total year-level sizes: 120, 110, 100, 90. Is this sample proportionate?

solution.en:
Proportionate stratified: each stratum contributes proportionally. Total students \(=420\). Sample size \(=40\).

Proportionate sizes: Yr 9: \(10/120\approx8.3\%\); Yr 10: \(10/110\approx9.1\%\); etc. Since each stratum contributes 10 (not proportional), this is disproportionate stratified sampling. Each stratum has equal representation but not in proportion to population size.

problem.en: An online poll on a news site asks visitors "Do you support the new tax?" 78% say no. Comment on the reliability.

solution.en: This is a voluntary response sample — readers choose to respond. People who feel strongly (especially those who oppose the tax) are more likely to participate. The 78% figure cannot be generalised to the general population. Results are biased.

body.en:
A school wants to know students' opinions on a new homework policy. The principal surveys only students who volunteer to respond. Identify the sampling method and any bias.

This is voluntary response sampling. Students with strong opinions (likely opposed to more homework) are more likely to respond, creating response bias and making results unrepresentative of all students.

Researchers want to test whether a new fertilizer increases crop yield. Describe a well-designed experiment.

Randomised comparative experiment: (1) Use 40 identical plots of land. (2) Randomly assign 20 to treatment (new fertilizer) and 20 to control (standard fertilizer). (3) Measure yield at season end. (4) Compare means. Random assignment controls for confounding variables.

question.en: Explain the difference between an observational study and an experiment. Can a well-designed observational study establish causation?

solution.en: An experiment imposes a treatment on subjects and randomly assigns them to groups; an observational study observes without intervention. Observational studies cannot establish causation because confounding variables cannot be controlled — only experiments with random assignment allow causal conclusions.

question.en: A pharmaceutical company is testing a new headache medication on 120 volunteers (60 males and 60 females). Because males and females often metabolize medications at different rates, researchers suspect biological sex may affect the response. (a) Describe an experimental design that incorporates blocking. (b) Explain why a randomized block design is preferable to a completely randomized design in this situation.

solution.en:
(a) Design: Form two blocks of 60 subjects based on biological sex: Block 1 (60 males) and Block 2 (60 females). Within the male block, randomly assign 30 males to receive the new medication and 30 males to receive an identical placebo. Similarly, within the female block, randomly assign 30 females to the new medication and 30 to the placebo. After a fixed period, measure pain relief in all subjects and compare the treatment and control outcomes within and across blocks.

(b) Justification: Blocking on biological sex accounts for and isolates the variability in pain relief attributable to metabolic differences between sexes. By comparing medication to placebo within each homogeneous block, researchers reduce unexplained variation (error variance), making it easier to detect a true treatment effect if one exists.

question.en: A city council member wants to gauge resident support for building a new public park. The council member sets up an online survey link on the municipal website and announces it during a local television news segment. Identify the sampling method, describe two specific sources of bias, and explain how the results are likely skewed.

solution.en:
Sampling method: Voluntary response sampling (convenience sampling).

Sources of bias: (1) Undercoverage: Residents without regular internet access, elderly citizens, or those who do not watch the local evening news broadcast have zero chance of participating. (2) Voluntary response bias: Individuals with strong opinions (particularly passionate advocates or staunch opponents of city spending) are far more likely to take the effort to visit the website and complete the survey than residents with neutral or moderate views.

Direction of bias: The proportion of respondents supporting or strongly opposing the park in the survey will be overrepresented relative to the true proportion across all city residents.
